What is a REL?

• A REL is a regional educational laboratory.
• There are 10 RELs across the country.
• The REL program is administered by the U.S. Department of
 Education, Institute of Education Sciences (IES).
• A REL serves the education needs of a designated region.
• The REL works in partnership with the region’s school districts, state
 departments of education, and others to use data and research to
 improve academic outcomes for students.

West Virginia Growth Model:
Changing Conversations about Student Performance

 Dr. Damian Betebenner
 Senior Associate
 The National Center for the Improvement of Educational Assessment

 7

West Virginia Growth Model
• The existence of annual student testing together with unique student
 identifiers forms the foundation for the calculation of student
 growth.
• Over the last decade, most states have begun calculation of
 longitudinal student growth using large scale state assessments.
• The analysis of student growth is controversial because of the uses to
 which it is put: Teacher & School Evaluation.
• Development of the West Virginia Growth Model involved the creation
 of a diagnostically useful quantity that could be used (or not used) at
 a later time for many purposes.

 8

West Virginia Growth Model
• Research on the SGP model began in 2007 (Betebenner, 2008)
• Based upon work in Colorado, the norm-referenced model was
 extended to include a criterion-referenced component. (Betebenner,
 2009)
• Work in other states incorporating the model into state reporting and
 accountability systems occurred in subsequent years and student
 growth became more common across state assessment systems.
 (Betebenner, 2012)

 9

West Virginia Growth Model
 Why Student Growth:

If you care about student achievement,
 then you care about student growth.

• Where you are is a function of
 where you started and how
 quickly you’ve travelled since.
• Student growth and student
 attainment/achievement are
 related in this way.
• Distance=Rate x Time
• Those who start behind tend to stay
 behind and those that start ahead
 tend to stay ahead.

 10

West Virginia Growth Model
• The concept of student growth isn’t as difficult to understand and
 popular perception suggests.
• Calculations may be complicated but knowing how to calculate
 student growth is not synonymous with understanding student
 growth:
 – The number π (pi=3.14159…) is difficult to calculate but is simple to
 understand conceptually.
 – Height and weight percentiles associated with children are difficult
 to calculate but are simple to understand conceptually.
• Computational details are important but often obscure a simple
 conceptual basis.

West Virginia Growth Model
• There are 3 general approaches of calculating student growth:
 – Growth as an amount of change (i.e., gain).
 – Growth as a norm/peer referenced quantity.
 – Growth as a criterion referenced quantity.

 13

West Virginia Growth Model
• Growth as an amount of change:
 – What could be more simple?
 – Like height or weight just calculate the amount of change.
 – Requires a vertical scale (which West Virginia has up to this year and
 will have going forward with SBAC).
 – Growth = Score Time 2 - Score Time 1

• Not as simple as it seems:
 – Comparisons between students often leads to wrong conclusions
 – Interpreting change requires context.

 17

West Virginia Growth Model
•This is analogous to height/weight measures for infants.
•Growth amounts are tricky to interpret and require context.
•Peer based comparisons used by growth analyses are a way to acquire that context.

 An infant male toddler is measured at 2 and 3 years of age and is
 shown to have grown 4 inches. The magnitude of increase—4 inches
 —is a well understood quantity that any parent can grasp and
 calculate at home using a simple yardstick. However, parents
 leaving their pediatrician’s office knowing only how much their
 child has grown would likely be wanting for more information:
 Parents are not interested in an absolute magnitude of growth, but
 instead in a norm-referenced quantity locating that 4 inch increase
 alongside the height increases of similar children.

 18

West Virginia Growth Model

• Peer-based analyses are also called norm-referenced analyses.
• Like with infant height/weight charts, peers are children/student
 with similar characteristics.
• For growth analyses using large scale assessments, peers are
 students with (at least) the same scale score history on the same
 tests.
• Peer based norms are invaluable in providing context for
 stakeholders to understand student growth.
• Peer based norms are possible even across test transitions like West
 Virginia’s transition from WESTEST 2 to SBAC.

West Virginia Growth Model

• Peer-based growth calculations are only as good as the assessments
 on which they are based.
• With quality assessments, peer based analyses can allow for all
 students to demonstrate growth.
• However, ceiling or floor effects on a test can impede the analysis of
 growth for students at the extremes.
• The goal is to be able to demonstrate for stakeholders student
 growth that is exemplary as well as that which is problematic.

 26

West Virginia Growth Model
• Growth is achievement over time

 27
 Source: West Virginia Department of Education/
 NCIEA

West Virginia Growth Model

• Peer based comparisons (norms) are helpful but limited by their
 very nature.
• One needs criteria as well as norms to have a complete
 understanding.
• A criterion-referenced interpretation examines the quantity against
 a set of standards.
• Student performance on the WESTEST 2 within the 5 performance
 levels and the new SBAC within the 4 performance levels are
 familiar examples of a criterion referenced interpretation of
 attainment/achievement.

 28

West Virginia Growth Model
• Growth is achievement over time

 29
 Source: West Virginia Department of Education/
 NCIEA

West Virginia Growth Model

• Criterion-referenced growth is also referred to as growth-to-
 standard.
• The standards used to examine growth are often the state’s
 performance standards.
• Peer based analyses (e.g., SGP) are used in many states as part of
 growth-to-standard analyses.
• Growth-to-standard analyses produce growth targets determining
 whether a student’s growth is sufficient to reach/maintain state
 standards.
• Absent norms, criterion-referenced growth produces results similar
 to achievement indicating:
 – Students that start behind tend to stay behind.
 – Students that start ahead tend to stay ahead.

 30

West Virginia Growth Model
• Most of the controversy surrounding student growth analyses centers
 on their (high stakes) uses:
 – Teacher evaluation
 – School evaluation/accreditation
 – Principal evaluation
• There is broad disagreement on whether results derived from state
 summative assessments are appropriate for personnel or
 institutional evaluation.
• Measures and uses often get conflated leading to push back against
 the measures (annual state assessments) themselves.
• States tailor their use of SGPs to their particular state policies.

 31

West Virginia Growth Model
• Like most states, West Virginia will transition to a new state assessment in
 2015.
• West Virginia is a part of the Smarter Balanced (SBAC) consortium and will
 use their test.
• The transition from the WESTEST 2 to SBAC have some impact on
 the growth analyses:
 – It will have minimal impact upon the norm-referenced analyses.
 – It will have a larger impact upon the criterion-referenced (growth-to-
 standard) analyses.
• Even with two distinct tests (WESTEST 2 & SBAC), it’s possible to
 monitor the relative progress of students.
• Monitoring growth-to-standard during the transition is more difficult
 for two reasons:
 – The standards have not been officially established
 – Data is not yet available on how students have progressed relative to
 the new test and standards.

 32

West Virginia Growth Model
• Growth is achievement over time

 33
 Source: West Virginia Department of Education/
 NCIEA

West Virginia Growth Model
• New tests, performance standards, and accountability systems have
 made the use of growth results for high stakes purposes even more
 controversial.
• Many states are diminishing/eliminating state assessment results
 from accountability calculations during the assessment transition.
 • New Jersey counts student growth as 10% of overall teacher
 evaluation in 1st year (versus 30% in later years).
 • Idaho postponing growth to standard results across assessment
 transition for school evaluation.
• Stakeholders often conflate the test itself with the use of the test.
• The challenges associated with the use of growth during the
 assessment transition are more about communication than about
 technical issues.

Purpose of A-F

• Provides clear and concise information on how well schools are
 doing
• Puts student achievement as the central focus of our education
 accountability and accreditation system
• Assists the Governor, the Legislature, the WVDE, and county boards
 of education in ensuring:
 – that high quality educational standards and annual performance
 measures and progress are met by all schools and school systems
 – and that a thorough and efficient system of schools is provided.

A-F Policy

Establishes an accountability system for West Virginia Public Schools
and an approval process for school systems based on:
(1) measures of student performance
(2) a system of reviews through which school and school system
 quality is examined and publically reported

Proficiency

Proficiency rates for mathematics and reading are calculated with the
following criteria for each subject independently.
• Students with full academic year (FAY) status
• Students enrolled in grades 3-11
• Students with a valid assessment result
• At least 10 FAY students for each subject at the school level

To calculate the proficiency components:
• Sum the number of students (that met the criteria above) that were
 proficient, and divide by the total number of students (that met the
 criteria above) for each subject.
• Multiply the proficiency rate for each subject by 200 to determine
 the number of points earned out of the total 200.

 67

Observed Growth

To calculate observed growth for each subject independently, the
following criteria must be met:
• Students Enrolled in grades 4-11
• Students who are FAY in the current year
• Students with valid scale scores in the current and prior year to get
 growth results
• 10 FAY students with growth calculations at the school level.
This calculation takes the sum of students with typical and high growth
by subject; then divides by the total number of students with growth
measures at a school by subject. Each rate is then multiplied by 100 to
determine the number of points earned out of the total 100.

 68

Adequate Growth

To calculate adequate growth for each subject independently, the
following criteria must be met:
• Students Enrolled in grades 4-11
• Students who are FAY in the current year
• Students with valid scale scores in the current and prior year to get
 growth results
• 10 FAY students with growth calculations at the school level.
This calculation takes the sum of students with a Yes indicator in either
the Keeping Up or Catching Up category for each subject (reading and
mathematics), then divides by the total number of students with
growth measures at a school by subject. Each rate is then multiplied by
100 to determine the number of points earned out of the total 100.

 69

Accelerated Growth

In order to calculate Accelerated Growth of the Lowest 25% of
students, first, the LOW25 subgroup must be identified.

 70

Identifying the LOW25 subgroup

To identify the LOW25 subgroup in a school, the following conditions
are to be satisfied independently for mathematics and reading scores:
• Students enrolled in grades 4-11 in the current year
• Students with a full academic year (FAY) indicator in the current
 year
• Students that take state assessments

 71

Low25 subgroup (cont.)

To calculate the LOW25 subgroup, the following steps will be taken for
reading and mathematics independently.
1. Count the total number of students who are FAY by grade level in
 the current year.
2. Determine the number of students in each grade that equals 25% of
 the accountable student population with growth results.
 – In cases where the result is a decimal, round up to the next whole
 number.
3. Using the students’ prior year scale scores, rank the students’
 scale scores from lowest to highest by grade.
4. Select the number of students as determined from Step 2
 starting with the lowest scale score.
 − If a student included in the LOW25 subgroup has the same scale
 score as a student(s) who just missed the 25% cutoff, include the
 student(s) in the LOW25 subgroup.

 72

LOW25 subgroup (cont.)

5. Set a LOW25 indicator for the students identified as the lowest
 performers in each grade.
6. Combine students indicated as being in the LOW25 subgroup across
 all grades into one LOW25 subgroup for the school.
7. If there are fewer than 10 students in the LOW25 subgroup, add an
 additional student participating in the state assessment per grade
 across all grades until the minimum of at least 10 FAY students can
 be met.

 73

Calculating Accelerated Growth

To calculate accelerated growth for each subject independently, the
following criteria must be met:
• A minimum of 10 FAY students in the LOW25 subgroup

Using current year growth results, calculate the accelerated growth
rate:
1. Sum the LOW25 students across grades that have High growth.
2. Divide by the total number of LOW25 students.
3. Multiple by 100 to determine the number of points earned out of the
 total 100.

Graduation Rates

• The certified graduation rates will be included as part of the A-F
 report card by converting the graduation rate to points.
• Graduation rates are certified during the October 1 Certified
 Collection for the prior year. These rates will then carry forward and
 be part of the report card for the year in which the rates are
 certified.
June 2014 graduates and Summer 2014 graduates are certified in
October 2014. The rates that are certified will be part of the score
card for the 2014-15 school year.

 75

Adding it Up!

• A school’s scores for each component will be summed as shown in
 prior referenced point value table.
• Schools will be ranked from highest points earned to the lowest
 points earned (elementary/middle schools will be ranked separately
 from high schools).
• Based on the points earned rankings, stanines will be calculated for
 elementary/middle schools, and stanines will be calculated for high
 schools in Year 1.

What is a stanine?

• Stanine (STAndard NINE) is a method of scaling test scores on a
 nine-point standard scale where the distribution of scores is divided
 into nine intervals and where the mean lies at the center of the
 fifth interval.
